beats.intro: Chapter six, lesson one. Studying cells. [[drop]]Look at a drop of pond water. It looks clear, but it is full of life. [[scope]]Put it under a microscope, [[push]]and the drop fills with tiny swimmers, each one a single cell. [[cell]]Every living thing is made of cells. [[ask]]How do we study something this small, and what is inside?
beats.ideas: Three ideas guide this whole chapter. [[basic]]First, the cell is the simplest collection of matter that can live. Every organism is made of cells. [[form]]Second, a cell's structure and its function are related. The shape of a part fits its job. [[prev]]Third, all cells come from earlier cells. A cell does not appear from nothing. It comes from another cell.
beats.scope: The tool that opened this field is the microscope. [[light]]The light microscope is the simplest type. Visible light shines through the specimen, the thing being viewed. [[lens]]Then the light passes through glass lenses, which magnify the image. [[eye]]The enlarged image reaches your eye, with detail that the unaided eye cannot see. [[more]]Electron microscopes use beams of electrons instead of light, and show finer detail still. The bacterium photo later in this lesson comes from one.
beats.frac: A microscope shows what a cell looks like. To learn what each part does, scientists use cell fractionation. [[break]]First, break the cells open. [[spin]]Then spin the mixture in an ultracentrifuge, a very fast centrifuge. [[layers]]The heaviest parts sink first, and the lighter ones stay in the liquid, so spinning faster in steps separates the organelles from one another. [[test]]Each separated batch can then be tested, using biochemistry, to see what chemistry it carries out. [[link]]Put those results together with the picture from the microscope, and you can link each organelle's structure to its function.
beats.q1: Quick check. What does the ultracentrifuge do in cell fractionation?
beats.shared: Now the big divide. [[all]]Every cell, of every kind, has four things in common. [[pm]]A plasma membrane around the outside, which controls what moves in and out. [[cytosol]]Cytosol, the semifluid inside. [[chrom]]Chromosomes, which carry genes. [[ribo]]And ribosomes, which make proteins. [[so]]Beyond those four, cells fall into two types.
beats.two: [[pro]]Prokaryotic cells belong to bacteria and archaea. The slide calls the second group archaebacteria, but today we say archaea. [[euk]]Eukaryotic cells make up protists, fungi, animals, and plants. [[size]]Eukaryotic cells are much larger. Many prokaryotic cells could fit inside one. [[nuc]]A eukaryote keeps its DNA in a nucleus, a compartment wrapped in a membrane. [[noenv]]A prokaryote has no nucleus. Its DNA sits in a region called the nucleoid, with no membrane around it. [[org]]A eukaryote also has many other membrane bound organelles, small compartments that each do one job. A prokaryote has none. [[cyto]]In a eukaryote, the cytoplasm is everything between the plasma membrane and the nucleus.
beats.ex: Try two cases. [[yeast]]Baker's yeast is a fungus, so it is eukaryotic. It has a nucleus, and organelles. [[coli]]E. coli is a bacterium, so it is prokaryotic. Its DNA lies in a nucleoid, and it has no organelles wrapped in membranes. [[same]]Yet both have a plasma membrane, ribosomes, and DNA. What differs is where the DNA sits, and how many compartments the cell has.
beats.bact: Zoom into one typical rod shaped bacterium. Bacteria also come as spheres and spirals. [[chr]]In the middle lies the bacterial chromosome, a long coiled DNA molecule. [[nuc]]The region it sits in is the nucleoid. One region, two names. [[ribo]]Ribosomes dot the cytoplasm, much smaller than the nucleoid. [[pm]]The plasma membrane surrounds the cytoplasm and controls what moves in and out. [[wall]]Outside it, the cell wall gives protection and support. [[cap]]Outside that, many bacteria have a sticky capsule, a protective outer layer. [[fim]]Short hairlike fimbriae help the cell attach to surfaces. [[flag]]And flagella are whip like parts that move the cell. [[scale]]In the micrograph, the scale bar is half a micrometer. That is the size for this one species, not for all bacteria.
beats.q2: Quick check. Is each feature prokaryotic, eukaryotic, or both?
beats.map: Now a preview of the tour ahead. [[cell]]This is a eukaryotic cell, an animal cell, and over the next lessons we visit each part. [[mem]]The plasma membrane bounds it. [[nuc]]The nucleus is the head office, holding the DNA. [[ribo]]Ribosomes are the workbenches that build proteins. [[er]]The endoplasmic reticulum is a production line, [[golgi]]and the Golgi apparatus is the shipping department. [[lyso]]Lysosomes are the recycling crew. [[mito]]Mitochondria are the power plants. [[cyto]]And the cytoskeleton is the scaffolding and rails that hold it all together. [[next]]Next lesson, we start with the nucleus and the ribosomes.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Cells are the basic units of life. Structure fits function, and every cell comes from an earlier cell. [[w2]]Microscopes show what cells look like. Cell fractionation separates organelles so we can test what each one does. [[w3]]All cells have a plasma membrane, cytosol, chromosomes, and ribosomes. [[w4]]Prokaryotes have a nucleoid and no membrane bound organelles. Eukaryotes have a nucleus and organelles, and are much larger. [[end]]Now try the practice.
